prompt.context: Your client is Tacotle Co., a leading national fast casual restaurant with $420M in revenue in 2014. Over the five years preceding 2014, Tacotle has experienced steady revenue growth and industry leading profitability. For the first time in its 15-year history, Tacotle has experienced three straight quarters of EBITDA erosion.
prompt.question: Tacotle's CEO has hired you to explore what is causing profits to drop and what can be done to reverse the tide.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been any changes in the competitive landscape?
clarifying_info.a: No major competitors have entered or exited; no new substitutes have been introduced; Tacotle currently holds a 30% market share by revenue, which it has maintained.

clarifying_info.q: How is the overall market doing?
clarifying_info.a: The market is growing at the same rate as GDP. It is a mature market.
Customers are beginning to stress the importance of ingredient quality and order customization.

clarifying_info.q: What is included in EBITDA / what does EBITDA mean?
clarifying_info.a: EBITDA stands for Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization. It is a measure of operating profitability.

clarifying_info.q: How did the average time to serve a customer change?
clarifying_info.a: The average time to serve a customer increased from approximately 1 minute to approximately 3.5 minutes.

exhibits.title: Tacotle Co. quarterly revenue and EBITDA
exhibits.shows: A bar/line chart showing Tacotle's quarterly Revenue and EBITDA from Q1 2012 through Q4 2014, with EBITDA % labeled for each quarter.

data.note: Revenue spikes in Q1 2014 then declines over subsequent quarters; EBITDA remains relatively flat before declining; EBITDA margin drops from ~45% range to ~39-40% range in 2014

exhibits.title: Tacotle Co. avg. revenue per order
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the average revenue per order over time, ranging from approximately $3.00 to $5.50.

exhibits.title: Tacotle Co. income statement
exhibits.shows: A three-year income statement (2012-2014) breaking out Revenue, COGS, Wages, Corp SG&A, Fixed Overhead, and EBITDA.

exhibits.title: Results of 2013 Tacotle Co. customer survey
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing customer-rated Importance vs. Tacotle's Performance across seven attributes for 2013: Quality, Speed of Service, Consistency of Product, Has a drive through, Restaurant Cleanliness, Friendliness of Staff, Ample Seating.

data.performance_scores: (bars shown; Tacotle lags on Quality relative to importance, on par or exceeding for other categories)

exhibits.title: Results of 2014 Tacotle Co. customer survey
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing customer-rated Importance vs. Tacotle's Performance across seven attributes for 2014. Note: the order of attributes has changed compared to Exhibit D.

data.performance_scores: (bars shown; Speed of Service is now Tacotle's weakest attribute relative to importance; Consistency of Product also below expectations; Quality now meets expectations)

framework: Declining EBITDA — root cause is internal, not market-wide
Market Conditions: competitive dynamics (new entrants, substitutes, market share), market growth/maturity, customer preferences
Tacotle Operations — Revenue: price changes, volume/units sold, product mix changes
Tacotle Operations — Costs: variable costs (COGS including ingredients, marketing, labor), fixed costs (PP&E, SG&A, fixed overhead)
Hypothesis: either a revenue-side shock (price increase drove short-term spike but volume declined) or a cost-side shock (COGS increase eroding margin), or both

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit A tell you about Tacotle's revenue and profitability trends?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note the Q1 2014 revenue spike followed by steady decline, EBITDA remaining relatively flat despite revenue spike (suggesting margin compression), and EBITDA % dropping from ~45% range to ~39-40% in 2014. Should hypothesize that either prices rose and/or units sold increased, but costs increased faster. Should ask what drove the revenue spike (price vs. volume) and why EBITDA margin fell.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit B tell you, and what follow-up question does it prompt?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that average price per order increased from ~$4.05 in 2013 to $5.25 in 2014. Should immediately note that a price increase could lead to a change in quantity sold and ask how unit volume changed.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits B and C, calculate the total number of units (orders) sold in 2013 and 2014. How did unit volume change?
questions.guidance: Candidate should derive units sold from Revenue divided by average price per order. Should conclude that despite a revenue increase, total units sold actually decreased — the revenue spike was entirely price-driven. Should then ask why units sold continued to fall through subsequent quarters.

math.setup: Units sold = Revenue / Average price per order
steps: 2013: Revenue = $377M (round to $380M); Avg price = $4.05 (round to $4); Units = $380M / $4 = 95M units
2014: Revenue = $420M; Avg price = $5.25 (do not round); Units = $420M / $5.25 = 80M units
Change: units fell from 95M to 80M, a decrease of 15M units despite higher revenue
Conclusion: the revenue spike in 2014 was driven entirely by the price increase, not by volume growth; units sold actually declined
math.answer: Units sold fell from ~95M in 2013 to ~80M in 2014 (-15M units, ~-16%)

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit C, what drove the EBITDA erosion from a cost perspective?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that COGS nearly doubled ($54M in 2013 to $96M in 2014, an increase of $42M) while all other cost lines were essentially flat. COGS is the root cause of the EBITDA margin compression. Candidate should ask why COGS increased so dramatically and speculate that ingredient costs rose (menu change).

math.answer: COGS nearly doubled and is the sole driver of EBITDA margin erosion; all other cost lines were flat.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit D tell you about Tacotle's operational performance vs. customer expectations in 2013, and what might Tacotle have done in response?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that in 2013 Tacotle lagged on Quality relative to its importance (highest-rated attribute at 4.8) but was on par or exceeding expectations for all other categories. Should conclude that Tacotle likely implemented a change aimed at improving quality — such as upgrading ingredients or adding menu customization — which would explain the COGS increase and price hike.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit E reveal, and what conclusions can you draw comparing it to Exhibit D?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize Exhibit E is the same survey repeated in 2014 (post-menu change). Key observations: (1) the attribute order changed, with Speed of Service now the most important factor; (2) Speed of Service is now Tacotle's weakest attribute — performance fell well below importance; (3) Consistency of Product also dropped below customer expectations; (4) Quality now meets expectations. Net effect: the menu change improved Quality but degraded Speed and Consistency, resulting in overall customer dissatisfaction and driving the volume decline seen in the calculations.

questions.prompt: List at least 5 cost drivers specific to the fast casual restaurant industry, broken down by fixed and variable.
questions.guidance: Candidate should demonstrate industry knowledge. Variable: food/ingredient costs (COGS), packaging, hourly labor, marketing/promotions, distribution/supply chain. Fixed: rent/occupancy, salaried management, equipment/PP&A depreciation, corporate SG&A, technology/POS systems. Should note that COGS (ingredients) is the dominant variable cost driver in fast casual and explains the sharp increase observed.

brainstorming.prompt: What operational changes could Tacotle have implemented that would cause both COGS to nearly double and the average price per order to increase?

categories.name: Menu changes
ideas: Increased customization options requiring more ingredient variety
Premium topping upgrades across all items
Expansion to new menu categories (e.g., adding proteins)

categories.name: Supply chain / sourcing
ideas: Switched to higher-cost suppliers for quality ingredients
Moved to organic or locally-sourced ingredients
Reduced scale efficiencies by diversifying supplier base

categories.name: Operational complexity
ideas: Added preparation steps requiring more labor time
More complex food assembly increasing wait times
Higher ingredient spoilage from expanded SKUs

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: Price increase passed through to customers to offset higher COGS

recommendation: Scale back the menu changes that were implemented in 2014
Focus the menu on a curated set of high-quality, customizable options that can be prepared quickly and consistently
risks: Scaling back the menu too much could reduce customer satisfaction for Quality, which is the second-highest importance attribute in 2014
Implementing a scale-back could disrupt supplier relationships and may require divesting assets purchased for the menu change at a loss
A scale-back that does not focus on margin improvement could reduce revenues and profits, effectively downsizing the company
next_steps: Perform more detailed and focused customer surveys to gauge what Tacotle customers expect from the chain
Perform a menu scale-back focused on cost-cutting balanced with customer needs
Future menu changes should be piloted on a trial basis at a small number of individual restaurants before chain-wide rollout
